sec.title: Background
sec.p: Wound healing is a complex process requiring coordinated cellular responses. Honey and silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) are well-known for their potential to heal wounds. However, there is little evidence of their combined impact on wound healing in fibroblast cells. This study aimed to investigate the combined effects of two types of honey with AgNPs on bacterial growth inhibition and wound healing in human dermal fibroblast cells.

sec.title: Method
sec.p: Honey samples were characterized based on phenolic content, antioxidant capacity, and protein levels. The AgNPs were synthesized and characterized by dynamic light scattering, ultraviolet-visible, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray powder diffraction. Antibacterial activity was assessed by checkerboard assay. The effect of honey, AgNPs, and their combination on fibroblast cell viability and wound healing was evaluated. Quantitative real-time PCR was conducted to evaluate the mRNA expression of growth factors.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Our results showed that Barberry honey significantly increased fibroblast cell growth, wound healing, and expression of FGF2, TGFβ1, COL1A1, and VEGFA genes compared to commercial honey. Combination of honey with AgNPs significantly increased VEGFA gene expression compared to either agent alone. Barberry honey and AgNPs also showed strong antibacterial effects individually. However, their combination had no synergistic effect.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: These findings suggest that Barberry honey and its combination with AgNPs could serve as effective agents for promoting the fibroblast wound healing process. However, more in vitro and in vivo research is needed to investigate further mechanisms of Barberry honey alone and in combination with AgNPs in wound healing.
Keywords: Wound healing, Honey, AgNP, Fibroblast, Combination, Antibacterial, Gene expression

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The skin, as the body’s primary barrier, is essential in defense against environmental pathogens. Disruptions in skin integrity compromise this barrier function, increasing susceptibility to infection and, in severe cases, leading to systemic complications [1, 2]. Wound healing is an intricate, multi-phase process involving hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and tissue remodeling with each phase requiring coordinated cellular responses [3]. Fibroblasts play an essential role throughout the healing process, particularly during the proliferative phase, by producing extracellular matrix (ECM) components, cytokines, and growth factors necessary for tissue repair [4, 5]. Effective wound healing depends on the migration and proliferation of fibroblasts, which lay the groundwork for new tissue formation [6, 7].

Honey has long been recognized as a therapeutic agent in wound care, owing to its diverse bioactive compounds, including carbohydrates, vitamins, amino acids, phenolic acids, and flavonoids. These compounds contribute to its potent antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and tissue-regenerative properties, which are influenced by seasonal and geographical variations [8, 9]. Honey’s high osmolality, acidity, phenolic compounds, and non-peroxidic elements give it potent wound-healing capabilities [10]. These properties enable honey to accelerate the healing process, decrease reactive oxygen species (ROS), promote wound debridement, improve angiogenesis, and effectively fight microbial infections [11–13]. Honey also has a beneficial effect on fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and keratinocytes’ cellular responses, promoting re-epithelialization and enhancing tissue regeneration [14, 15].

Similarly, silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) are getting a lot of attention for their unique properties in wound healing [16]. Large surface area allows AgNPs to release large amounts of silver ions, which can penetrate damaged skin and increase their therapeutic potential [17]. These nanoparticles possess potent antibacterial properties that are crucial for enhancing the wound healing process. By targeting specific metabolic pathways, they disrupt critical functions in microorganisms, such as DNA replication and protein synthesis [18]. AgNPs effectively prevent biofilm formation and combat multi-drug-resistant bacteria, making them particularly valuable in managing complex wounds [19]. Additionally, AgNPs enhance wound healing by modulating inflammation [20, 21] and promoting cell proliferation [22], thereby creating a more favorable environment for tissue repair.

Honey and AgNPs are widely recognized for their applications across various fields [23–25]. Combining these two agents may enhance their therapeutic properties through synergistic effects. While several studies highlight individual benefits of honey and AgNPs in wound healing [26–28], limited data exists on their combined effects, particularly in stimulating the expression of key growth factors. Successful wound healing depends on the complex relationships between cytokines, growth factors, cells, and signaling pathways [29]. Important growth factors in this process include basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), epidermal growth factor (EGF), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and transforming growth factor-beta 1 (TGF-β1). These factors are essential for cellular communication because they control reactions such as cell migration, proliferation, and differentiation, all of which promote effective wound healing [30]. Therefore, this study aims to investigate the combined effects of two types of honey, differing in quality, with AgNPs on bacterial growth inhibition. It also examines their potential to enhance the wound healing process in fibroblast cells by evaluating cell migration and the expression of key growth factors.

sec.title: Honey sampling
sec.p: Barberry honey was obtained from local beekeepers in the Zohan region of South Khorasan Province, Iran during the spring season. Commercial honey was purchased from a local market. The total phenolic compounds (TPC) and total antioxidant capacity (TAC) of honey samples were measured by Folin-Ciocalteu reagent (FCR) and 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) assays respectively using commercial kits of Zantox (Kavosh Aryan Azma Co, Iran).
The Bradford test was used to determine the total protein content [31]. Honey samples were classified as strong or weak based on their antioxidant capacity, phenolic, and protein contents.

sec.title: Synthesis and characterization of silver nanoparticles
sec.p: AgNPs were synthesized using a chemical reduction method based on the following protocol. Briefly, a 2 mM silver nitrate (AgNO₃, Merck, Germany) solution was prepared as the silver ion source. A 2 mM sodium borohydride (NaBH₄, Merck, Germany) solution was used as the reducing agent, and a 50 mM trisodium citrate (Na₃C₆H₅O₇.2H2O, Dr. Mojallali Chemical Laboratory, Iran) solution served as the stabilizing agent. A 50 ml AgNO₃ solution was maintained at low temperature, after which a (50:50 5 ml) mixture of NaBH₄ and Na₃C₆H₅O₇.2H2O solutions was added dropwise under continuous stirring. This process continued until a distinct color change to brown was observed, indicating the successful formation of AgNPs. The obtained nanoparticles were washed twice with distilled water and centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 10 min. Characterization of the synthesized AgNPs was performed using UV-Vis spectroscopy to confirm the characteristic surface plasmon resonance band of silver nanoparticles, dynamic light scattering (DLS) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to determine particle size distribution and morphology, and X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis to assess the crystalline structure.

sec.title: Minimum inhibitory concentration and minimum bactericidal concentration assay
sec.p: Gram-negative and gram-positive bacterial strains, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa (ATCC 27853), Escherichia coli (ATCC 15597), Staphylococcus aureus (ATCC 25923), and Enterococcus faecalis (ATCC 29212), were used in this investigation. The standard strains of bacteria were obtained from the Laboratory of Microbiology at Birjand University of Medical Sciences. All of the bacteria were grown on tryptic soy agar (TSA) at 37 °C. A 0.5 McFarland standard (1.5 × 108 CFU/ml) was used to standardize the bacterial suspension used in each assay.

The antibacterial activity of honey and AgNPs was assessed by determining the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) using the broth microdilution method according to Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute guidelines (CLSI, 2012) with necessary modifications [32]. Serial twofold dilutions of honey (ranging from 100 to 3.1% w/v) and AgNPs (ranging from 1000 to 1.9 µg/ml) were prepared in Mueller-Hinton broth (MHB). Subsequently, 10µl of the standardized bacterial suspension was added to each well of a 96-well microtiter plate (final cell concentration 5.0 × 105 CFU in well). Wells containing MHB alone served as negative controls, while wells with bacteria but without treatment served as positive controls. The microplates were incubated for 24 h at 37 °C. The MIC was visually determined based on the absence of turbidity in the well. The minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) of agents was determined according to the MIC values. 10 µl of each well exhibiting no growth was transferred to agar plates (MHA) and incubated at 37 °C. The lowest concentration of the agents at which incubated bacteria was inhibited was considered as the MBC.

sec.title: Checkerboard assay
sec.p: The checkerboard technique was used to evaluate the antibacterial interaction of honey and AgNPs in vitro [33]. Briefly, a series of dilutions was used to prepare a range of AgNPs concentrations (at least 4X MIC-1/8 MIC) and honey (100 − 15% w/v). Then, 95 µl of each AgNPs and honey concentration samples and 10 µl of bacterial suspension was added to each well of the 96-well plate (final cell concentration 5 × 105 cells/well) and incubated for 24 h at 37℃. The concentration of combination (AgNPs and honey) with no visual growth was considered as MIC in the checkerboard assay. To evaluate the interaction between honey and AgNPs, the fractional inhibitory concentration (FIC) index was calculated using the following formulas.

The FIC index was evaluated according to the following criteria: ≤0.5, synergistic interaction effect; >0.5 and ≤ 1.0, additive interaction effect; >1 and < 4, indifferent interaction effect; and ≥ 4, antagonistic interaction effect [34].

sec.title: Cell culture
sec.p: The Human Dermal Fibroblasts (HDF) were obtained from the Pasteur Institute Cell Bank (Iran) and were derived from the dermis of normal human neonatal foreskin. The cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) enriched with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and a 1% penicillin- streptomycin mixture (Gibco). Cells were cultured in a CO2 incubator (5% CO2) at 37 °C and exchanged media every 2–3 days to reach confluence.

sec.title: Cell viability assay
sec.p: HDF cells were seeded at a density of 15 × 103 cells in 96-well plates and incubated overnight at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO2. The cells were then treated with different concentrations of honey (0.31, 0.62, 1.25, 2.5, 5 mg/ml) and nanoparticles (0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8 mg/ml). After the treatment, 10 µl of MTT was added to each well, and the plates were incubated at 37 °C for an additional 3 h. Following MTT incubation, the purple formazan crystals were dissolved by dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (Merck, Germany) and the absorbance was measured by a microplate reader (Biotek Epoch, Winooski, VT) set to 570 nm with a reference wavelength of 630 nm [35].

sec.title: Scratch wound healing assay
sec.p: A scratch assay was conducted to assess the property of honey, AgNPs, and their combinations to promote cell migration and in vitro wound healing. HDF cells were seeded at a density of 2 × 105 cells/well in 12-well plates and cultured until they reached subconfluence. A scratch was made using a sterile 100 µl pipette tip, followed by washing with PBS. The cells were then treated with the test samples, and images of the wound area were taken at 0, 24, and 48 h to assess cell migration and closure [36].

sec.title: Quantitative real time-PCR
sec.p: Total RNA was extracted from cells using the Parstous kit (Tehran, Iran). The concentration and purity of RNA samples were measured using the Nanodrop System (Biotek Epoch). The isolated RNA was then utilized for cDNA synthesis with the Parstous kit (Tehran, Iran), in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Expression levels of VEGF, TGFB1, FGF2, and COL1A1 were quantified using an Amplicon SYBR Green PCR Kit (Amplicon, Denmark) and Applied Biosystems Step One Plus real-time PCR instrument. The sequences of the primers are presented in Table 1. The target genes expression was quantified using the 2−ΔΔCt method, relative to the housekeeping gene GAPDH [37].

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis and graph construction were performed using GraphPad Prism version 9.4.19 software (GraphPad Software, Inc., La Jolla, CA). The data are expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (SD). Differences among more than two groups were analyzed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by Tukey’s post-hoc multiple comparison test. For comparisons between two independent groups, such as the compositional analysis of Barberry honey and commercial honey, an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test was used. A p-value of < 0.05 was regarded as statistically significant.

sec.title: Biochemical analysis of honey samples
sec.p: In this study, honey samples were evaluated based on their TPC, TAC and total protein levels. Biochemical analysis of honey samples was shown in Table 2. The results showed that Barberry honey exhibited higher levels of phenolic compounds (215.21 ± 4.2 mg gallic acid (GA) per 100 g honey), antioxidant capacity (74.73 ± 2.03 µM Trolox equivalents (TE) per 100 g honey), and total protein content (116.03 ± 6.32 mg per 100 g honey). In contrast, commercial honey had lower values for these parameters, with TPC, TAC, and total protein content measuring 35.43 ± 0.81, 2.14 ± 0.3, and 39.04 ± 1.5 mg per 100 g honey, respectively. Based on these findings, Barberry honey was classified as a strong sample, while commercial honey was categorized as a weak sample.

sec.title: Characterization of silver nanoparticles
sec.p: The characterization of the nanoparticles is shown in Fig. 1. The UV-Vis spectrum exhibited a characteristic absorption peak at 417 nm, confirming the successful synthesis of AgNPs through surface plasmon resonance (SPR) vibrations. DLS measurements indicated a hydrodynamic size of approximately 54 ± 1.3 nm, while TEM images revealed that the AgNPs were spherical with an average diameter of 20.19 ± 4.08 nm. In addition, the zeta potential of the nanoparticles was measured as −21.44 mV, indicating their colloidal stability. The XRD analysis displayed diffraction peaks at 2θ = 38.27°, 44.41°, 64.62°, and 77.44°, corresponding to the (111), (200), (220), and (311) crystal planes, respectively. The XRD pattern shows no additional peak, which denotes the formation of a pure silver nanoparticle.

C TEM image illustrating morphology and particle size (scale bar = 50 nm). D XRD pattern confirming their crystalline structure

sec.title: Antimicrobial activity of the compounds
sec.p: The MIC and MBC of honey and AgNPs samples against E. coli, P. aeruginosa, S. aureus, and E. faecalis bacteria are provided in Table 3. Barberry honey showed better antibacterial effects compared to commercial honey. The lowest MIC was observed for Barberry honey against S. aureus (12.5%) and P. aeruginosa (25%), while commercial honey had a higher MIC (≥ 50%), indicating weaker antibacterial activity.

caption.p: MIC and MBC of honeys and AgNPs against tested bacteria

sec.p: In comparison, AgNPs showed stronger antibacterial activity. The lowest MIC values ​​were observed against the gram-negative bacteria P. aeruginosa (31.25 µg/ml) and E. coli (62.5 µg/ml). However, both tested honeys and AgNPs showed limited effects against E. faecalis with MIC values ​​greater than 50% of honey or 500 µg/ml of AgNPs. The profile of MBC values ​​for Barberry honey and AgNPs was very similar to the MIC values. In most cases, MBC values ​​were equal to or slightly higher than the MIC (one higher dilution). For commercial honey, MBC values ​​were generally higher than the MIC values, indicating a weaker bactericidal effect compared to Barberry honey and AgNPs.

To evaluate potential interactions between honey and AgNPs, the checkerboard assay was employed. The combination of Barberry honey (12.5%) and AgNPs (31.25 µg/ml) yielded an FIC value of 0.75, indicating an additive effect against E. coli. Similarly, the combination of commercial honey (25%) and AgNPs (31.25 µg/ml) produced an FIC value of 1, which also reflected an additive interaction against E. coli. In contrast, for the other tested bacteria, including S. aureus, E. faecalis, and P. aeruginosa, both types of honey in combination with AgNPs demonstrated indifferent effects, with FIC > 1 values (Table 4).

sec.title: Effect of honey and silver nanoparticles on the viability of human dermal fibroblast cells
sec.p: In current study, the effect of two types of honey and AgNPs and their combination on the cell viability of HDF cells was investigated using MTT assay. Agents at different concentrations were applied to HDF cells for 24 h, and cell viability was measured. As illustrated in Fig. 2, low Barberry honey concentrations (0.31 mg/ml) showed no significant cellular changes. At 0.62 mg/ml, a statistically significant (p < 0.05) slight increase in cell viability was observed. A more pronounced effect emerged at 1.25 mg/ml, revealing a significant difference (p < 0.001) compared to lower concentrations. Cell viability at 2.5 and 5 mg/ml remained significant but marginally decreased relative to the 1.25 mg/ml concentration. Commercial honey at concentrations of 0.31 and 0.62 mg/ml demonstrated no substantial impact on HDF cell viability, maintaining levels comparable to the control group. Higher concentrations elicited a statistically significant (p < 0.05) modest increase in cell viability compared to lower dosage ranges. Our results also demonstrates that AgNPs at 0.5–4 µg/ml did not significantly alter cell viability. However, 8 µg/ml AgNPs induced concentration-dependent cytotoxicity (p < 0.001). Combination therapy demonstrated nuanced effects: Barberry honey + AgNPs consistently enhanced cell viability (p < 0.001), while commercial honey combinations maintained near-control cell viability. Notably, 0.5 µg/ml AgNPs showed increased cell viability, whereas 8 µg/ml concentration significantly decreased cellular survival. Based on these findings, subsequent experiments utilized a standardized combination of 1.25 mg/ml honey and 4 µg/ml AgNPs.

sec.title: Effect of honey and silver nanoparticles on wound healing in human dermal fibroblast cells
sec.p: The effect of honey and AgNPs alone and their combination on wound healing in HDF cells was evaluated using scratch wound healing assay. The obtained images and calculated wound closure rates are shown in Fig. 3. After 24 h, all treated groups exhibited a significantly higher wound closure rate compared to the control group (38.64%). Among them, AgNPs alone also demonstrated a statistically significant effect (46.65%, p < 0.01), while the other treatments, including honey and their combination with AgNPs, showed even greater enhancement, with wound closure rates ranging between 47.69% and 72.66% (p < 0.001).

caption.p: A Wound healing activity of different treatments on HDF cells with the scratch assay from 0 h to 48 h of incubation. B Quantification analysis and the percentage of wound closure in the different treatment groups (* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001 compared with control)

sec.p: After 48 h, the wound closure percentage continued to increase across all treatment groups. However, the improvement was not statistically significant for the AgNPs and commercial honey groups compared to the control. Interestingly, the commercial honey with AgNPs group showed a modest but statistically significant increase (p < 0.05). The most pronounced enhancement was observed in the Barberry honey (95.13%) and Barberry honey + AgNPs (89.45%) groups, both of which exhibited highly significant wound closure rates (p < 0.001).

sec.title: Effect of honey and silver nanoparticles on mRNA expression of wound-healing genes in human dermal fibroblast cells
sec.p: The impact of honey and AgNPs on mRNA expression levels of key wound-healing genes (FGF2, TGFβ1, VEGFA, and COL1A1) in HDF cells is illustrated in Fig. 4. For FGF2 gene expression, treatment with Barberry honey, both alone and in combination with AgNPs, resulted in a significant upregulation compared to the other groups (p < 0.001). However, other treatments did not show statistically significant changes in FGF2 expression. Our results showed that all treatment groups caused significant upregulation of TGFβ1 mRNA expression when compared to the control, except for the AgNPs-treated group, which showed no statistically significant difference. In addition, we found that combination treatments led to an upregulation of VEGFA gene expression compared to the control. The combination of Barberry honey + AgNPs produced the most pronounced increase, with a 3.2-fold change (p < 0.0001). However, commercial honey alone did not induce a significant change, while its combination with AgNPs elevated the VEGFA gene expression (p < 0.05). Moreover, Barberry honey (p < 0.01) and its combination with AgNPs (p < 0.05) showed significant increases in COL1A1 gene expression. Commercial honey also elevated the level of COL1A1 expression in HDF cells (p < 0.05), while in the combination group, the effect wasn’t significant.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In current study, we investigated the effect of two types of honey and their combination with AgNPs in dermal fibroblast-mediated wound healing and their antibacterial effect in vitro. Our findings indicate that Barberry honey has significant effects on various dermal fibroblast-mediated wound healing functions. Notably, AgNPs enhanced the effects of honey on angiogenesis-related genes, indicating that honey modulates the response of dermal fibroblasts to low-dose AgNPs via the wound healing signaling pathway.

Many studies have documented the broad-spectrum antibacterial activity of honey and nanoparticles [38, 39]. In the present study, the MIC and MBC of honey and AgNPs were assessed against bacterial strains. The results revealed that MIC and MBC values for E. coli and P. aeruginosa were the same in Barberry honey but differed in commercial honey, suggesting strong bactericidal activity of Barberry honey. Similarly, Al-Sayaghi et al. demonstrated identical inhibitory (MIC) and bactericidal (MBC) concentrations for Sidr honey (50%) and Manuka honey (30%) against E. coli [40]. In contrast, differing MIC and MBC values have been observed in other studies, highlighting variability in the bacteriostatic and bactericidal effects of honey. For instance, the MIC of Sidr honey against E. coli was reported to be 10% (v/v), while the MBC was 40% [41]. AgNPs demonstrated strong activity against E. coli and P. aeruginosa bacteria, with MIC and MBC values ranging from 31.25 to 62.5 µg/ml. These findings are in line with earlier studies showing that gram-negative bacteria are more susceptible to AgNPs than gram-positive bacteria [42].

The studies demonstrated that AgNPs could improve the effectiveness of natural agents against bacteria [43]. The synergistic and additive effects of combining Oregano essential oil with AgNPs against multidrug-resistant bacteria were demonstrated by Scandorieiro et al.‘s study [44]. Similarly, Alkawareek et al. reported the synergistic activity of AgNPs combined with hydrogen peroxide against E. coli and S. aureus [43]. In contrast, the combination of AgNPs with β-lactam antibiotics showed an indifferent effect on S. aureus bacteria [45]. Guruvu et al. have investigated the effectiveness of the combination of multifloral honey with AgNPs against urinary pathogens. They reported that the combination is effective against E. coli, P. mirabilis, and P. aeruginosa bacteria [46]. Although no synergy was observed in this study when honey was combined with AgNPs, the combination exhibited additive effects against E. coli but had an indifferent effect on other bacterial strains.

The wound-healing process is an intricate biological process involving inflammation, angiogenesis, re-epithelialization, granulation tissue formation, and ECM remodeling [47]. In the early stages, fibroblasts play a crucial role by proliferating, migrating to the wound site, and synthesizing new ECM while differentiating into contractile myofibroblasts [48]. Various compounds have been investigated in the wound healing process using fibroblast cell models [49, 50]. In this study, honey was shown to enhance cell viability in the specific doses. Notably, Barberry honey, as well as its combination with AgNPs, exhibited superior efficacy in promoting cell viability compared to commercial honey. This enhanced effect is likely attributed to the higher levels of antioxidants, polyphenols, and proteins found in Barberry honey. Previous research has also highlighted the role of phenolic compounds in honey on cell viability, supporting the observed findings [51]. Additionally, AL-JADI et al. demonstrated that the stimulatory effect of honey on cell proliferation was significantly higher than that of a sugar solution. This suggests that sugars act as a source of energy and contribute to the stimulatory action of honey. However, the wound-healing effects of honey are not only due to its sugar content but also result from other bioactive compounds [52].

Fibroblast migration and proliferation are essential for effective wound healing. In order to evaluate the wound healing potential of honey, we conducted a scratch assay. Our findings revealed that HDF cells exhibited enhanced migration toward the artificial wound when treated with Barberry honey. This suggests that compounds in Barberry honey may promote wound healing by stimulating fibroblast migration. A similar research on different honey from Romania reported that its total phenolic and flavonoid content stimulated the migration of keratinocytes and enhanced fibroblast proliferation [36]. Pinocembrin, as a flavanol in multifloral and orange honey, accelerates the in vitro healing of skin wounds by directly stimulating keratinocyte migration. Interestingly, pinocembrin modulated the production of inflammatory cytokines, including IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-10, by inhibiting the activation of nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) [53]. Furthermore, the honey’s ability to heal wounds might be linked to an immune response regulation, which Pinocembrin would modulate [54].

Our results demonstrated that AgNPs accelerated wound closure and could help honey in closing the wound. This aligns with the findings of You et al., who stated that low concentrations of AgNPs promoted wound healing [55]. Similarly, Cataldi et al. demonstrated that combining vitamin D3 with AgNPs facilitates wound closing [56]. In another study, Abbasi et al. (2021) reported that 0.2% AgNPs ointment improved wound healing in animals [57].

Studies on the combined application of propolis and honey in wound healing found no synergistic effect on fibroblast proliferation and migration in vitro [26, 58]. However, this combination significantly enhanced and accelerated wound healing in vivo [13, 59]. This discrepancy may arise from the complexity of the in vivo environment, where multiple cellular and biological processes interact to facilitate tissue repair [60]. In vivo, the combination of propolis and honey supports angiogenesis, granulation tissue formation, and epithelialization, all of which contribute to faster wound closure [13]. Additionally, their synergistic antimicrobial properties help control infections, creating an optimal environment for efficient healing [61].

Fibroblasts, the primary cell type in the dermis, produce ECM components and growth factors such as EGF, FGF, TGFβ, collagen, etc. These substances are the key regulators of the wound healing process and contribute to ECM regeneration [62]. During the process of wound healing, collagen plays a vital role in inducing significant cellular events such as ECM remodeling [63].

Research on natural products for wound healing has also shown their potential to enhance collagen production [64, 65]. For example, polyphenols such as resveratrol enhances collagen synthesis and promote epidermal and dermal repair in mouse models [66]. Chaudhary et al. demonstrated that Manuka and Jamun honey dilutions significantly upregulated the expression of collagen types I and III in treated fibroblasts [67]. During open wound healing, fibroblasts differentiate into myofibroblasts under the influence of the ECM, contributing to the synthesis of collagen types I and III. This fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition plays a vital role in wound healing by promoting collagen production [68]. In another study, Iosageanu et al. found a significant increase in collagen synthesis in an in vitro fibroblast model treated with meadow multifloral and honeydew honey. This enhancement in collagen production was positively correlated with the flavonoid and total phenolic content of the tested honeys, suggesting that honey’s bioactive compounds contribute to its wound-healing properties [36]. Similarly, Salvo et al. reported that medical-grade honey (Ulmoplus®), when combined with copper nanoparticles (CuNPs), significantly enhanced fibroblast activity and the synthesis of type I and III collagen fibers in both infected and uninfected wounds. These findings affirm that the combination of CuNPs with Ulmoplus® promotes collagen fiber maturation, supporting more effective wound healing [64]. In our study, collagen gene expression was increased in honey groups and Barberry honey combined with AgNPs.

Growth factors play a crucial role in wound healing, and our research shows a strong correlation between wound healing activity and growth factor modulation. Barberry honey, which exhibited the most potent effects on cell proliferation, also significantly upregulated the expression of key growth factors in fibroblast cells, including FGF2, TGFβ1, and VEGFA. The involvement of these factors in wound healing has been previously documented [49, 69]. The Aloe vera can increase the production of TGFβ1 and bFGF, which will stimulate the collagen deposition, angiogenesis, and fibroblast proliferation [49]. Moreover, the combination of Aloe vera flower and gel synergistically induced HDF cell proliferation, migration, and ECM formation by upregulating TGF-β, α-SMA, and MFAP4 expression through the activation of the extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) and AKT signaling pathway [50].

The ability of honey and AgNPs to increase the expression of VEGFA shows the effect of their combination in wound healing. This is consistent with previous research that highlight the crucial role of TGFβ and VEGF in accelerating wound healing [70]. Recent research has shown that AgNPs increase the protein expression of PDGF and VEGF, which are essential for effective wound healing [71]. Another study demonstrated that the enhancement of VEGF and TGFβ gene expression has a remarkable effect on wound healing by increasing angiogenesis, thus promoting the healing rate. AgNPs have also been found to modulate the inflammatory response after injury by regulating cytokine levels [72]. Ambrožová et al. reported that non-cytotoxic concentrations of AgNPs (0.25 and 2.5 µg/ml) have a positive impact on the wound healing process by decreasing the NF-κB and IL-6 expression and activating the nuclear factor (erythroid- derived 2)-like 2/heme oxygenase-1 (Nrf2/HO-1) pathway in HDF cells [73]. These findings demonstrate that AgNPs at non-toxic concentrations can promote wound closure through multiple pathways, indicating its complex and potentially beneficial role in wound healing.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study demonstrates that honey, particularly Barberry honey, and its combination with AgNPs positively influence fibroblast migration and the expression of key genes involved in wound healing. Barberry honey alone showed the most pronounced effect on growth factor gene expression, while its combination with AgNPs notably enhanced VEGFA expression. These findings suggest that Barberry honey, both individually and in combination with AgNPs, holds therapeutic potential for accelerating wound healing and tissue regeneration. Nevertheless, additional in vitro and in vivo studies are necessary to elucidate the underlying mechanisms in greater detail.

sec.title: Limitation
sec.p: While this study provides valuable insights into the antibacterial and wound healing effects of two types of honey, alone and in combination with AgNPs, several limitations should be acknowledged. Firstly, artificial honey (sugars only) was not included as a control in the experiments, which could help better clarify the role of non-sugar components. Secondly, the molecular mechanisms underlying the observed effects remain unclear and require further detailed investigation. Thirdly, the experiments were conducted only in vitro using HDF cells, which may not fully replicate the complex biological environment of wound healing in vivo. Future studies involving animal models and focused on molecular mechanisms are necessary to confirm and expand upon these findings.
